item.title: Nothing More than Tools?
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: My psychological defenses kept retreating as frontier LLMs entered mathematical research. Are these models really nothing more than tools? I must rethink what gives meaning to my mathematical life. The core is what I would call toolization—keeping humans at the crucial nodes of the intellectual activity while outsourcing parts of the reasoning.
item.content:encoded:
Chenmin Sun, CNRS junior researcher at UPEC

I have subscribed to a commercial LLM for more than three years, at $20 per month. As a Chinese native living abroad, I used it to polish my language, to seek advice on daily life concerns, and to chat about almost anything. It was a toy, sometimes a friend who could patiently listen to me, and most of the time a shortcut tool. It entered my mathematical life at the beginning of 2025, when I could play with it in the context of university-level problem-solving, interactively learning papers from other domains in which I had little expertise. The model, accessible to me through that cheap subscription, evolved at almost a constant pace. It became my custom-made super search engine, calculator, verifier and reliable Wikipedia.

As a PDE researcher dealing with many estimates, I had always expected a real-time research assistant embedded in my workflow while editing a long paper in LaTeX. It would perfectly understand the logic flow I was working on, helping me to deal with tedious case checks and basic estimates where the guiding principle is clear. At that time (even at the beginning of 2026), LLM agents were not that popular in my community, and it was difficult—at least for me—to implement the above workflow. AI for mathematics remained distant from my research. It was not yet the assistant I had hoped for.

The situation changed dramatically over the past few months. While news about AI-solved Erdős problems kept coming, the storm was getting closer to all of us. The first wave of preprints emerged on arXiv, with many AI-solved (or heavily-assisted) mid-to-high-profile problems in every domain of mathematics. It was the time of GPT-5.5, and since then we have seen GPT-5.6, Fable 5, Astra… People devised a dazzling array of ways to play with these models: first, all kinds of prompting tricks that seemed to lack intellectual depth; then workflow construction and the distillation of various skills. In early 2026, building agent tools still posed a certain barrier to entry for non-programmers. But once Codex and ChatGPT were deeply integrated, an amateur who knew nothing about mathematics or programming could, with nothing more than naive prompts, keep a model working until an oracle-like proof was spat out by the computer. So, are these agents built on frontier LLMs really nothing more than tools?

By common sense, a tool is characterized by a specific range of uses and a determinate capability—or at least by a capability that improves steadily within a predictable range. Motivated by a desire to understand the performance of a frontier commercial model, I tried one a couple of months ago. My psychological defenses kept retreating: An early version (GPT-5.5) could not solve any of the problems in a small set from my personal collection. The situation changed when GPT-5.6 arrived. To understand which “hard problems” were worth working on, I started testing several open problems in my field—fortunately without success. Later in the summer, I heard about a fancy way of working—so-called “drawing cards” for major open problems. People around me were drawing cards, and succeeding. From my perspective, this way of working is hallucinogenic. We immerse ourselves in a virtual world as commanders of a massive army, commanding well-equipped soldiers (agents) to attack day after day until they exhaust their ammunition (tokens), with only very high-level intervention. Even pure curiosity—the will to know the truth—chases us, and hallucination emerges in our minds: we must know; we will know. An invisible force catches us: well-organized prompts must be sent before leaving home, during dinner with family, and before sleep. Does any tool make us addicted like that?

The ethical consequences are even more serious. If a result is obtained through long but almost context-free prompts, whose name should appear on the paper? Opinions differ. From my perspective, authorship of a research article—as distinct from an expository article—should be reserved for those who contribute creative intellectual input. And in the case of automatic problem-solving, where the model works essentially on its own to close the loop of theorem-proving and verification, why should it be credited only as a tool?

This is no longer hypothetical. On October 6, 2026, before the community could adapt to the new paradigm at a reasonable pace, OpenAI released mathematical manuscripts grouped into 372 result families, including candidate solutions to high-profile problems across all areas of mathematics. The news came like a cluster of nuclear bombs, destroying the old landscape of mathematics, yet few survivors could foresee the new horizon.

This is the landmark event that forces me to confront an existential crisis. There is no more room for psychological retreat. I must rethink what gives meaning to my mathematical life.

Without getting involved in the controversial commentary on similar events, or in how we should act collectively, I would rather share my individual thoughts on how I want to adapt to the advance of AI in my career. Since nobody can predict the future, I should state that what I am going to discuss should not be taken as a standard or judgement I am imposing on others, and these views will steadily evolve over time.

The core is what I would call toolization. More specifically, the model is assigned a bounded range of local tasks, while humans pilot the direction at crucial nodes of the search tree. However, the definition of local tasks and the direction of the search vary from person to person, and will also evolve over time. A tricky integral at the undergraduate level is a local task for an experienced researcher who understands the mechanism behind it, but it remains a good training exercise in a master’s internship project. We can take it for granted that we may outsource labor within our ability. For instance, suppose there are two scale-invariant estimates for a given integral, A and B. We applied A, while the model applied B to get a better bound. It does a nice job as a co-pilot, and we advance more quickly. In current PDE research, what is essential is the architecture and the mechanism of how things work. For example, one must conjecture a blow-up profile, construct an ansatz to close the bootstrap, design fine norms to encode linear/multilinear effects, and guess Lyapunov functionals. We pilot these directions, and suitable AI tools (not just prompting LLMs) would allow us to quickly test ideas and counterexamples, to code for numerical experiments, to use knowledge from other domains, and to carry out the dirty work.

Mathematical development is based on the compression of concepts. Just as nowadays researchers directly use theorems of Banach spaces or classical analysis without opening the black box of the proof, AI tools allow us to work on modules, compressing not only a specific theorem in the literature, but also low-to-middle levels of reasoning. Yet, unlike traditional compression, which rests on clear definitions, the compression of AI reasoning requires novel conceptualization, so that similar mechanisms can be generalized and reused. As part or even all of the reasoning is outsourced, conceptualization becomes a new kind of cognitive work for human mathematicians, increasingly decoupled from the problem-solving process.

In another direction with the same principle, an LLM is a mobile library and a custom-made teacher. Learning ideas and techniques from other fields (even outside mathematics) in which we have no expertise, digesting new results (human or AI-produced), and coding become more convenient. This way, again, it is our consciousness that decides what to understand, and how deeply to understand it.

I acknowledge that it is always difficult to get toolization right, given the continuously increasing mathematical capabilities of LLMs. In the research process, a more delicate situation arises when an LLM contributes a key idea. It leads us towards a new direction—one that turns out to be successful—that we had not previously considered. If that happens, I consider the LLM a collaborator who deserves credit. This would make me excited, because I could reach further horizons that would otherwise be difficult to find on my own, while also making me feel a sense of loss. After all, making creative contributions to the process of discovery is a principal motivation for why I do mathematics.

As a double-edged sword, long interaction with an LLM might cause reliance on it that deskills us, eroding our abilities and intuition. But I think this effect can only be evaluated a posteriori, over time. I could periodically ask myself a set of questions: Do I gain a better understanding of my subject? Am I still able to do AI-free mathematics when I am on the plane? What cognitive tasks can I safely outsource to a model? Ideally, these questions would help me maintain both intellectual growth and independence. The critical dose of AI usage depends on the person. As we now have models with a wide range of capabilities, choice and discipline become a new personal challenge.

Today, it is becoming clearer that the industrialization of mathematics is coming; nobody is sure whether it will be a golden age of discovery or a regression of civilization. It depends on the collective narrative and on individual practice. We need time to adapt to the new paradigm, to reach a certain consensus within our community, and to rebuild our confidence. The destructive impact is real, but one thing is certain: mathematics is not a closed system, and human curiosity about the universe is unbounded.

Received 10 October 2026.

item.title: Postdoc Hiring in the Age of AI: What Still Matters (and a Call for More Advice from Those Doing the Hiring)
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: Alessio Figalli and Sobhan Seyfaddini, drawing on their experience hiring postdocs, explain how they will evaluate candidates this year in light of recent AI advances. They will privilege substance over publication counts and expect an in-depth mathematical conversation at interview. More advice from those doing the hiring will be added here.
item.content:encoded:
SERIES · Part of our application-season series for people considering a PhD, doing a PhD or looking for a postdoc. We expect a few more contributions like this one from people involved in hiring this year, and welcome others (send us yours); they will be added to this post as they arrive. Applicants can ask questions in the comments below. Each contribution reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

Alessio Figalli and Sobhan Seyfaddini, Professors at ETH Zurich

Drawing on our experience as past and current members of postdoctoral hiring committees, we would like to share our perspective on how to evaluate postdoctoral candidates in the age of AI.

AI does not change what we ultimately want to assess in a candidate: the depth of their mathematical understanding, the substance of their own contributions, and their potential to develop new ideas.

At the initial shortlisting stage, we expect recommendation letters and CVs to play an important role, but we do not regard publication counts alone as a reliable guide to a candidate’s potential. We are more interested in the substance of the work and in what the application reveals about the candidate’s own contributions, ideas, and development as a mathematician. Where possible, we may also examine selected papers more closely to gain a better understanding of the mathematical ideas involved and how they are presented.

For shortlisted candidates, the interview will be crucial for assessing their mathematical understanding and judgment more directly.
Can they explain the ideas behind their results, why the arguments work, and where the difficulties lie?
Can they discuss what they tried, what failed, and which questions remain open?
We would also like to understand how they see their work in a broader mathematical context, why they consider it significant, and what they regard as their own main contributions. We expect that a talk followed by an in-depth discussion will give us a good sense of each candidate’s mathematical understanding, maturity, and approach to research.

Our advice to applicants is therefore to make their own contributions clear in their applications and to be prepared to discuss their work in depth, since a thoughtful and honest mathematical conversation can reveal far more than a publication count. While the ways in which we assess candidates may evolve as the tools available to mathematicians change, our emphasis will remain on mathematical understanding, originality, and research potential.

Received 5 November 2026.

item.title: It’s a great time to be an amateur mathematician
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “In early August, I was at TIFR Mumbai for an ‘AI for Math’ conference. This is one of many such events happening in mathematics departments all over the world in recent times. Among the speakers was Dinesh Thakur. In his talk, he described how he had received an email from an auto mechanic in France about a conjecture attributed to him. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Nihar Gargava, Postdoctoral researcher at Université Paris-Saclay

PS: I used AI for speech-to-text, proofreading, and locating references. I thank Dinesh Thakur for comments on an earlier draft.

In early August, I was at TIFR Mumbai for an “AI for Math” conference1. This is one of many such events happening in mathematics departments all over the world in recent times. Among the speakers was Dinesh Thakur. In his talk, he described how he had received an email from an auto mechanic in France about a conjecture attributed to him2. The email came with a disproof of this conjecture about primes over function fields that he had written about in 2015. What was surreal about this incident was that the person sending this counterexample did not even know what finite fields are! He had just asked Claude (Opus 4.8) to find a “precisely stated conjecture about polynomials with some examples worked out and something that can be checked by computations”, quoting Dinesh. Dinesh told us that eventually the author did learn more about the problem via more prompting. The preprint is currently on arXiv3.

The reaction from the audience was quite dramatic. There was laughter in the room, but also shock and disbelief. Two reactions that I recall were “what does it mean to have any expertise anymore?” and “it’s a great time to be an amateur mathematician”. By mid-October, these stories are becoming more common, and I expect that trend to continue. I would like to present my thoughts about this.

Mathematics is full of delightful stories of outsiders making an impact. The most famous is that of Ramanujan, whose letters to Hardy still bring pleasure to the mathematics community even after repeated readings. It seems to me that every professional mathematician at one point in their career must have gotten an email from a Ramanujan-wannabe. Most of these are bogus emails and we don’t bother replying to them. But now these emails are getting smarter and more intricate because of AI. Firstly, a crackpot with a crazy claim can now instead run his ideas through a language model and spare a mathematician a few bytes of mailbox space. Secondly, a mathematician can receive an interesting piece of mathematics tailor-made to appeal to their taste.

I recently had my Ramanujan-Hardy moment myself when Michael Simkin, who lives in Georgia (the country), sent me a new lower bound on sphere packings in high dimensions. The model’s write-up was an astonishing mess that would be difficult to read for any poor soul having to go through it, perhaps more so for Michael, who is mostly an outsider to research mathematics. He asked AI to recommend a mathematician who could verify the result, and it gave him my name.

When Michael reached out to me, I did get interested. At first, I thought he was Michael Simkin, the lecturer at MIT. But after a few emails I realized this was someone else. The output from the model had nice tricks to make progress on some of the ideas that I had long abandoned. So I asked Michael if he would like to coauthor this with me. I also (with his permission) added a PhD student to this project—Matthias Gröbner (because who owns AI-generated results?). The preprint is now out on arXiv4.

I wanted to understand what had drawn Michael to this problem, so we talked about it. Michael told me that he had been interested in mathematics since high school. He grew up in Tel Aviv and had even won an IMO bronze medal in his teenage years5. Mathematics has kept him going in life, even though his parents could not afford university education for him. Michael is now known for interesting life form constructions in Conway’s Game of Life6. For the past few years, he had been living as a digital nomad all over the world, finally settling in Georgia. These days he works part-time for a brain imaging center. He is proud of his AI-prompting skills and wants to keep helping mathematicians.

I asked Michael what he thought about expertise in mathematics and whether he felt that he could replace mathematicians with his AI chats. He had an answer that I found pretty nice. Coming from a software engineering background, he knows the feeling of AI being able to do the job better than humans. But he adds “as a programmer, I still have skills that are important but I cannot pinpoint what they are”. I guess this is quite close to what mathematicians feel.

The post-AI age could be a good time for mathematicians to reach out to people like Michael. It could be of mutual benefit. Not only do people outside want to understand what the mathematics produced by the models is saying, but we might also need them to understand how the public sees and interacts with mathematics. Human mathematicians should exist to talk about mathematics to humans, and the humans are finally reaching out in our mailboxes. They are finally speaking our language and learning about our work at their own pace. I think we should engage with at least some of them as a kind of individual outreach. AI might be taking away some of the fun parts of our jobs, but there might be new opportunities in our mailboxes.

The following are my thoughts as of now, and I expect to keep updating them as interactions between professional and hobbyist mathematicians become more common in the AI era.

Advice to hobbyist mathematicians

It might look as though mathematicians spend most of their time going through the gory details of individual lemmas and propositions in papers. In practice, however, mathematicians often focus on the few parts of a paper that are genuinely novel or interesting, without checking every detail once they are convinced that the result should be true. Much of the communication of mathematical ideas also happens through conversations between mathematicians, who have developed a shared language for talking about what matters in a proof. My advice to hobbyist mathematicians is to be patient with and respectful of this process. Try to understand how mathematicians communicate with each other, and learn to talk about your own ideas in that language. Being imperfect is okay, but trying will earn you a lot of respect.

Advice to professional mathematicians

The goals of hobbyist mathematicians might sometimes seem outrageous or too far removed from those of a professional researcher. They might be especially keen to be the first to prove a theorem, improve a bound, or put a result into the world just to have their name on it. But these could be respectable ambitions and, pre-AI, were (often tacitly) shared by many professional mathematicians. Even when we do not share precisely the post-AI goals of human understanding, there is still an opportunity for collaboration between hobbyists and professionals. Professional mathematicians should be mindful of their own priorities while respecting hobbyists’ expectations.

Addendum: Michael’s new homepage is 7

  1. Tata Institute of Fundamental Research. AI for Math workshop programme. (2026). ︎
  2. D. S. Thakur. Fermat-Wilson supercongruences, arithmetic derivatives and strange factorizations. arXiv:2211.01076 (2022). ︎
  3. D. Niedbala Giraudin. A counterexample to a conjecture of Thakur on Carlitz-Wieferich primes. arXiv:2607.15305 (2026). ︎
  4. N. Gargava, M. Gröbner, & M. Simkin. A cyclotomic gluing construction for lattice sphere packings. arXiv:2610.12619 (2026). ︎
  5. International Mathematical Olympiad. Individual results – Israel. ︎
  6. LifeWiki contributors. Michael Simkin. ︎
  7. M. Simkin. Personal homepage. ︎

item.title: I’m Not Done Doing Math! Don’t Ignore Me!
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “But I am still interested in doing math. I still think my research direction has genuine merit, and I still feel like I have more mathematics to give to the world. Thanks to AI, it is now feasible for someone like me to keep going.” […]
item.content:encoded:
Anonymous, Math PhD student

SERIES · AI is making papers cheap to produce but they remain costly to referee. Proofs and Prompts is publishing a series of posts from 26 October on the future of publishing, papers and credit. Questions such as how to disclose AI use, who bears the cost of checking, what authorship means and what papers of the future might look like will be addressed. This post is part of the series. Each is written independently and reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

I am about to graduate with a math PhD, with zero published papers, and a subpar thesis that’s just barely enough for me to graduate.

I have no illusions that I am on the same intellectual tier as the tenured professors, postdocs, and PhD students much more successful than me writing on this blog. I am no Yitang Zhang. I readily admit that I am a low-level mathematician compared to even the peers in my department. And much of this is my own fault. Significant stretches of my time in the program were spent procrastinating and being distracted, not to mention just plain being stuck on a project because I wasn’t good enough.

Realistically, I will not, and should not, be getting a research postdoc. I will end up in an overloaded teaching position or working a regular 9-to-5 job. And I do not have contempt for this future. I am sure I will manage to find a job that is fulfilling for me.

Under the old rules of academia, my life in mathematical research was over. I was supposed to quietly pack up my stuff, and leave research mathematics to the REAL mathematicians.

But I am still interested in doing math. I still think my research direction has genuine merit, and I still feel like I have more mathematics to give to the world. Thanks to AI, it is now feasible for someone like me to keep going. With language models accelerating the time-consuming parts of research, it is realistic for someone carrying a heavy teaching load or working a day job to produce novel, interesting mathematics in the little free time they have.

That is what I am going to try to do. And what is wrong with that?

I wanted to write this down because when I read essays here, whether pro-AI or anti-AI, people like me aren’t considered a part of the conversation.

We have an opportunity right now to ‘catch’ the people who have fallen by the wayside. People who just barely survived their PhD program and still have good ideas. Or people with just a Master’s or a Bachelor’s in mathematics who didn’t want to go through the grueling 5+ years of low pay for a PhD. Or those that went through years of postdoc positions and failed to secure a tenure-track job. We, the people outside of research academia that still wish to continue with mathematical research, exist!

But almost every conversation among established researchers seems to forget that. This is understandable because, before AI, many of us could not feasibly do serious research mathematics outside of a research position. Research math is incredibly time-consuming. Even if someone had a novel mathematical insight, keeping up with the latest literature, checking citations, and writing things up in an understandable, presentable way was a time-consuming process. It was not feasible to do without a lengthy dedicated research time in their schedule, afforded by a research position. We were not considered “real mathematicians” for a good, understandable reason. (There are exceptions, of course. Those outside of research jobs have produced a great deal of amazing research before AI. But we must admit that it is now MUCH EASIER to do research math outside of an academic position.)

Now, with the advent of AI, it IS realistic for us to continue participating in mathematical research.

So could we be brought back into the conversation?

Because right now, when I read through the posts on this blog, people like us are completely ignored:

  • I see reports from elite gatherings like the Harvard CMSA summit on Math and AI, or calls for societies to set norms. Will those boards and summits ever include people like me? Will they care about the opinions of an overloaded teaching faculty member just wanting to continue exploring the direction of their thesis? Or the person doing math research in their free time after their 9-to-5? I am afraid that these organizations will just be another society of already successful mathematicians writing rules for themselves.
  • There is some panic that AI will create a torrent of papers and there simply won’t be enough qualified people to peer-review them. Really? There aren’t enough people to review them? Thousands of math PhDs graduate every year without continuing a research career. Is there really a shortage of capable people, or is our definition of “capable” severely restricted? With AI, it is now much easier for those without research positions to keep up with the latest developments in their fields. Would that not drastically INCREASE the number of qualified peer reviewers?
  • Several pro-AI posts suggest that because AI makes writing papers too easy, we should stop writing papers or devalue them in favor of live seminar talks and in-person workshops. Do people realize how exclusionary this is? It is a luxury that can only be afforded by those with grants and dedicated time off for travel.
  • I see professors warning that because of AI, we might “lose an entire generation of mathematicians”, while others decry that AI will reduce math from a profession to a mere “hobby” done in people’s spare time. Where was this panic when the academic job market was throwing away the vast majority of every graduating PhD class for decades? And why is doing math in your spare time, for zero money and zero career credit, treated with such contempt?

I have lost the game of academic research careers, and I have made peace with that fact. What frustrates me is that the mathematical research establishment pretend I don’t exist. When a tool finally comes along that lets me keep doing the thing I love, making small but real contributions to my field from outside of a research position, I continue to be ignored. Instead, one side is telling me that my work doesn’t count for using AI, while the other side talks only about how it can be directed to better serve and preserve the scant few dedicated research positions.

It is telling that even in a fictional utopian vision of mathematics in 2038, set in a literal post-scarcity world, one can only imagine the mathematical community through the eyes of... an ETH Zurich professor and a postdoc heading to a three-month retreat in Princeton. Wow. Just wow. Even in the wildest, most utopian fantasies of the future, people like me don’t exist.

Received 1 November 2026.

item.title: Futures of Maths Launch
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: Today we launch Futures of Maths, a new, living platform that asks the mathematics community about the most pressing questions around maths and AI.
item.content:encoded:
Francesco Fournier-Facio, Assistant Professor at Heriot-Watt University; Yara Kyrychenko, Research Fellow at University of Cambridge (St John’s College); Jon Roozenbeek, Associate Professor at University of Cambridge and VU Amsterdam; Julian Wykowski, Postdoctoral Researcher at Karlsruhe Institute of Technology

Today we launch Futures of Maths, a new, living platform that asks active research mathematicians about the most pressing questions around maths and AI. A string of solutions to famous maths problems, found with the help of AI, has provoked a great deal of discussion among research mathematicians. We built Futures of Maths to understand how mathematicians are dealing with this change in their research and teaching, and where they see the field heading.

How it works. The platform shows you short statements about maths and AI. You rate each one from “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree”, or skip it, and you can mark the ones you find exceptionally important. Once you have answered, you see how everyone has rated the statement so far. You don’t have to finish in one go: you can leave and come back at any time. Most importantly, you can post your own statements. A moderator checks each one, and then everyone else can rate it, so the set of statements keeps evolving with the community’s input.

Results. Once we have collected enough responses, we will publish the results and make them available to the community. We will post again on Proofs and Prompts when this happens.

Who can participate. You can take part if you are 18 or older and have at least one article published in the last 5 years in a mathematics journal, meaning one indexed by zbMATH Open (recently accepted articles also count). The quickest way in is to sign in with ORCID. The article must be on your public ORCID record, added by Crossref. Articles you enter yourself don’t count. If it isn’t there, accept Crossref’s permission request in your ORCID inbox and make the work public. If that doesn’t work, for example because your article is accepted but not yet published, you can request a manual review from your institutional email address. We review these case by case.
We appreciate that this is only an approximation of what an active research mathematician is, but we chose it for its simplicity, objectivity and efficient verifiability. We welcome proposals of alternative criteria that cover a more representative sample, and have these same three qualities, they could be implemented in future iterations.

Privacy. The survey is anonymous. Verification happens on a separate website, and the survey itself never learns your name, email address or ORCID iD. When you first register, you receive a personal link that lets you return as often as you like as the consultation evolves. Please save this link. We can’t look it up or resend it, because that is what keeps you anonymous. Questions about yourself are optional, under “My session”, and you can withdraw your answers at any time.

Inviting wide participation. The results will only be meaningful if a large and diverse group of people takes part, both proposing statements and rating them. Please share this widely, and especially with people whose point of view you feel is underrepresented in the discussion on maths and AI.

If you have any suggestions or feature requests, please leave them in the comments!

Received 5 November 2026.

item.title: Reject the Neurosis, and Terrible Messaging, of our Loudest Voices — The Case for (Ir)rational Optimism
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “If you look up AI and math on any news site, you will read statements including ‘AI is destroying careers’ or ‘AI is nuking entire areas of math’ or even a prominent Field’s medalist saying ‘I cried so hard due to AI in math that I woke up my daughter’. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Anonymous, Postdoc

If you look up AI and math on any news site, you will read statements including “AI is destroying careers” or “AI is nuking entire areas of math” or even a prominent Field’s medalist saying “I cried so hard due to AI in math that I woke up my daughter”. The news loves a good headline, and these extreme statements make for good headlines. Underneath these articles is the comment section, with many comments hostile to mathematicians. One comment read “Imagine being a seven year old and your father waking you up to cry that other people did math problems.” This comment, hostile to mathematics (and arguably bad faith), I think sums up a very common reaction of non-mathematicians to some of these articles. I wanted to argue with this commenter, but I realized that this reaction was, on some level, perfectly reasonable if you just read the article and were not a mathematician.

It is no secret that graduate students can be stressed out and neurotic. I have been talking to younger mathematicians, and some are taking the rhetoric of senior mathematicians very seriously. I feel badly for them — some are incredibly depressed. I’m not going to tell people how to feel, because this is pointless. However, I do try to be more balanced than senior mathematicians have been — both because I think it is correct, but also because I have been disgusted by poor leadership.

The purpose of this essay is to implore senior mathematicians to tone down the extreme rhetoric, especially when communicating with the media and with junior mathematicians. I am encouraging this both because I believe these extremes aren’t true, but more importantly because it is bad leadership. It is like going into battle, even if you’re all going to die, your captain shouldn’t cry to you about it.

One major effect AI will have is forcing us to move on from well-trodden ground. The Riemann hypothesis has been around since…well…Riemann. The Navier-Stokes equations were introduced in the early to mid 1800s. Since then, these problems have accumulated an immense amount of prestige. Maybe it is time to move on? There are new questions to ask, there are new theories to develop, and new math to do. It seems like a lot of the neurosis comes from senior mathematicians who have attached an inordinate amount of self-worth to solving specific, well-formulated, and difficult conjectures. This is just one style of math, and it should not be seen as the entirety of math. AI will force a shift away from this style, which will ultimately lower the prestige attached to certain areas. However, in my personal opinion, this is a very good thing. I welcome this shift.

A second major effect AI will have is an increase in the number of papers, particularly incremental or “slop” papers. This is unequivocally bad. This may have a silver lining though — hopefully paper counts will be devalued, and paper quality will be valued more. This is a good thing.

A third major shift, related to the second, is that we can no longer trust someone’s papers to accurately represent their understanding or ability. This, again, is bad. However, similarly, I hope that this makes other things emphasized more in assessment — chalk talks, qualifying exams and coursework in grad school, informal conversations, and so on. The grad school standard of publication being the most important has, in my opinion, gotten a bit out of control. One thing a PhD should qualify you to do, is to teach mathematics. At the bare minimum, a person with a PhD in mathematics should be able to teach any undergraduate mathematics class or core graduate mathematics class (analysis, algebra, and geometry) with little difficulty. In reality, I don’t know how common this is. I hope AI devalues “novel contribution” and increases the value on having a solid foundation of core areas of mathematics.

Beyond any of these specifics, I have a very strong prior in the belief “nothing ever happens”. Mathematics has been around for thousands of years; it has undergone many changes. This will be yet another change, and mathematics will come out the other side alive.

If you still aren’t convinced, then could you at least tone it down a touch when talking to the media and younger mathematicians? If we really are marching towards the mathematical equivalent of nuclear armageddon, it is the responsibility of senior mathematicians to maintain some level of calm.

Received 24 October 2026.

item.title: In Defence of Incremental Mathematics
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: AI makes useful incremental mathematics easier without making it less valuable. Leading journals could add electronic daughter journals and pay referees, expanding trusted publishing capacity, and bolster familiar institutions for expanded demand.
item.content:encoded:
Anna Maltsev, Reader in Applied Probability at Queen Mary University of London

SERIES · AI is making papers cheap to produce but they remain costly to referee. Proofs and Prompts is publishing a series of posts from 26 October on the future of publishing, papers and credit. Questions such as how to disclose AI use, who bears the cost of checking, what authorship means and what papers of the future might look like will be addressed. This post is part of the series. Each is written independently and reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

At the end of the Royal Society’s recent conference on AI and mathematics, Professor Ben Green said, “The vibe today has been a lot more positive and sort of forward-looking,” and I found myself thinking, “Did we just attend the same meeting?” It didn’t feel very positive to me. The optimism was quite cautious, while the atmosphere of panic was shrill.

There was a session on publishing in that meeting and I asked a question. The question was whether perhaps we could split the mathematics journals into a flagship and daughter journals, like Nature. At coffee someone told me the question was provocative. It was not meant to be. It seems to me to be a very natural idea: if the publication system is under strain, we could expand it by having more journals. Encouragingly, someone else said to me also at coffee that it was a very good idea.

A lot of people seem to think that it’s a good idea to just destroy the publication system and try to do something better. Politicians do say, “Never waste a good crisis.” But we are not politicians. We are in a crisis, but we don’t have to use this revolutionary time, which is profoundly changing how we do mathematics, to also revamp the publication system at the same time. An alternative is to bolster the publication system as it is. The new generation will be writing and publishing their research probably in larger quantities, and so will we, the more senior academics. Then, once the AI crisis is weathered and the dust settles a bit, we can go back to having those slow deliberate discussions about revamping the publication system that we’ve been having for a while.

There is this idea floating around that we are seeing the death of mathematics. I think that we are not. I hope we will be instead seeing an acceleration and flourishing of mathematics. The purpose of this essay is to defend the value of incremental research even if it is easy and to flesh out some details of the idea that I suggested in the question at the Royal Society AI meeting as to how all the worthy incremental research might be published. A deep philosophical existential crisis that has a practical solution that maintains the status quo and just takes a bit of money, as this one does, is not quite as poignant as crises could be.

Why the problems we work on are important

In every paper and every grant application, I write why the problems I work on are important. Here is a paragraph from a grant application from last spring:

“We know from numerics and experiments that many complex physical systems demonstrate the same behavior independently of the precise details of interactions among their constituent elements. This phenomenon, called universality, is conjectured to hold more generally. In the context of random matrices, the universality conjecture asserts that various properties of large random matrices are independent of the precise probability densities that govern their stochastic behavior. This conjecture has deep philosophical and practical consequences, allowing random matrix theory to be applicable in a wide variety of contexts. Two well-known examples are in data analytics (e.g., Principal Component Analysis), where both data and noise come from an unspecified non-Gaussian distribution, and in nuclear physics where the randomness models the complexity of a large atomic nucleus. Thus random matrix universality fulfils one of the central objectives in mathematical physics: the derivation of macroscopic properties of large systems, despite unknown or random specifics of interactions.”

In this paragraph I set out why the problems I study are important: the philosophical question of why large system behaviour doesn’t depend on nitty-gritty details and how someday this kind of thing may be applied. None of these justifications are impacted by the fact that the research will now be easier to carry out.

I believe the importance of mathematical results comes from understanding, but that’s a rather overused word. What exactly is meant by understanding? There are a few things that make mathematics and mathematical results important. One of them is shining light on the structure of various mathematical objects. We may think of the themes of structure and randomness in Prof. Terence Tao’s blog and eponymous book: what is structure, what is randomness, how one turns into the other, and finding structure in various interesting and unexpected places. The second is to tell apart—and this is done by rigorous proofs—what is always true, what is sometimes true, what can be true and in what pathological cases it is true, and what is always false, and also to tease out which aspects contribute to a behaviour and which don’t, i.e. which assumptions are used and which are not necessary.

Mathematics looks very far forward. If it was cancer research thus accelerated, there would not be so much gloom. While we are not curing cancer, the technologies we now use are based on mathematics developed decades, if not centuries, ago. Mathematics is very forward-looking. In 500 years, maybe, the technology humanity will be developing will be based on the mathematics done now.

Incremental research

Incremental research is important for various reasons. I don’t believe that breakthrough research is truly possible without the availability of wide variety of results and methods. Consider Perelman’s proof of the Poincaré conjecture, announced in 2002–03. It followed the Ricci-flow programme that Richard Hamilton had begun in 1982. Between Hamilton’s starting point and Perelman’s breakthrough lay a growing body of results: existence and uniqueness theorems, Shi’s local derivative estimates, Hamilton’s compactness theorem and the Hamilton–Ivey curvature estimate. Among papers on these subjects many were incremental. These gave mathematicians tools for controlling the flow and understanding its singularities. Perelman built on this accumulated theory.1

For most of us, while we mustn’t tell this to our funders, we may honestly say that a lot of papers we write are incremental. I think of breakthrough research like spires on a church, which is built upon the little bricks, brick by brick, of incremental papers. For those bricks to be useful, there needs to be somewhere for them to be placed. The way we publish incremental research will affect all of us, but particularly early-career researchers, PhD students and undergraduates, who usually start with high-quality incremental research. They used to take joy in it, get credit for it and get training from it. If all of that research just collects dust in people’s hard drives, that will be a profound loss to mathematics.

More research needs more capacity

I am finding myself two to three times more productive now that I use ChatGPT than I used to be and solving problems I tried and failed to solve before. If this gain is generalised to the community, we can expect two to three times more papers to go through the publication system. The publication system is under strain.

Professor Martin Bridson, speaking in the afternoon of the same meeting, was talking about cups. He was saying that there are cups that go into museums, and then there are cups that we drink coffee from. I think, in his analogy, the cups we drink coffee from were the kind of incremental research that I am talking about here. He said they’re very important, and they are very important. But it’s even more useful to have these cups if they’re organised into cupboards. Currently, the journal system organises these cups by field and by quality, one way or another. It tells us where the cups from a particular field are, which cups are good, which are mediocre and which are bad. That is important for hiring, promotion and evaluation of people’s work. It is also important for readers.

Daughter journals and paid refereeing

A practical idea to expand publishing is to split high-profile math journals: use the big-name journal as a flagship and add five electronic daughter journals. The flagship would retain its present form and standards; the daughter-journals would provide homes for sound but more incremental work. They could be organised by subject, with their own editorial boards and shared administration. Nature provides a precedent. An early attempt to divide it into three publications in 1971 was reversed in 1974. The lasting expansion kept the flagship and added specialist titles, notably Nature Genetics in 1992, Nature Structural Biology in 1994 and Nature Medicine in 1995. The daughters inherited the Nature name and, with it, some of the prestige and confidence built up by the original brand. They did not have to attract authors and readers entirely from scratch. Historians of this expansion describe precisely this transfer of reputational capital through the shared name.23

The question voiced often is why not just use the arXiv? The answer to that is peer-review. ArXiv doesn’t have it. With the expansion of incremental research, can we find the capacity to peer review it? Thus a key to this idea would be paid refereeing. Right now, refereeing carries a cost and no benefit aside from some moral satisfaction. I believe that, with the cost-of-living crisis and housing crisis, there will be many more takers if the task is paid for. The advent of AI also makes refereeing easier. Part of the referee’s job is to verify that the arguments presented are correct and that the calculations presented are correct. The AI can do this quite well now. The human just needs to check whether the paper constitutes an advance, is important enough for a particular journal, and is well written.

Therefore, I believe that the use of AI in refereeing, as well as monetary incentives, can allow us as a community to cope with the reading and processing of papers and the sorting of them into cupboards, and thus building our field brick by brick but quicker and further.

What it would cost

One may ask about money. I had ChatGPT Astra cost an expansion of the Annals into one flagship and five daughter journals, with the daughters being online. The working assumption is 30 papers per daughter each year, or 150 additional papers per family. For the Annals, allowing 30 flagship papers gives 180 published papers annually across the family.

The report budget assumes two initial reports at £100 each per fully reviewed manuscript, a 50 per cent acceptance rate after full review across the whole family, and one revision report per accepted paper. That is five reports per published paper on average, including reports on rejected manuscripts. We then allow another 400 preliminary or additional reports per family each year. For the Annals family, this gives 1,300 reports, costing £130,000. The 50 per cent assumption is a family-wide rate after transfers, not the flagship’s overall acceptance rate.

Daughter-journal operations add £55,000 per family annually: £25,000 for a shared office and platform, plus £200 for light production on each of the 150 new papers. Adding a 10 per cent contingency gives £203,500 a year for the Annals family, with a further £50,000 to launch it.

For ten leading journal families (Annals of Mathematics, Acta Mathematica, Inventiones mathematicae, Journal of the American Mathematical Society, Publications mathématiques de l’IHÉS, Duke Mathematical Journal, Journal of the European Mathematical Society, Geometric and Functional Analysis, Annales scientifiques de l’École normale supérieure, and the CPAM/Courant family), the plan therefore creates 50 new electronic daughters alongside ten existing flagships: 60 journals in total. With 445 flagship papers and 1,500 new daughter papers as the planning volumes, the annual allowance is 13,725 paid reports. The totals are as follows.

So the answer is about two million pounds a year, with half a million to get started. It is not that much on the scale of research funding. Various foundations, like the Simons Foundation, governments and AI companies are plausible supporters.

Conclusion

Of political slogans, my preferred one at this interesting time is “Keep calm and carry on.” The research we have always been doing just got easier but, in my opinion, no less important. There have been discussions about improving on the journal system for a long time now, and we do all realise that it is not perfect. But it has functioned reasonably well for a long while and, with a little bit money and a dose of caution toward radical change, could function qualitatively in much the same way in an age of AI as it always had, but simply with expanded quantity. An acceleration of mathematics need not mean the end of the institutions that have served it.

AI Declaration

AI has been used to help polish and research this essay. Ideas are my own. Costing is fully AI generated.

  1. John Lott, The Work of Grigory Perelman, especially the account of earlier Ricci-flow results on pages 2–3. Read source ︎
  2. Nature, History of Nature. See the 1970s and 1990s sections for the early split and the later specialist titles. Read source ︎
  3. Mahdi Khelfaoui and Yves Gingras, Expanding Nature: Product line and brand extensions of a scientific journal, Learned Publishing 35 (2022), 187–197. DOI: 10.1002/leap.1422. Read source ︎

Received 3 November 2026.

item.title: Picasso rephrased: AI is useless
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “Pablo Picasso (1881-1973): ‘Les ordinateurs sont inutiles. Ils ne savent que donner des réponses.’ Cited in many places, but the source is unknown. Thus it may be fictitious. But ‘AI is useless. It only knows how to give answers.’ points to, in my opinion, one of the biggest steals inherent in the OpenAI post from 6 October 2026. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Joachim von zur Gathen, Retired professor of computer science at the University of Bonn

Pablo Picasso (1881-1973): “Les ordinateurs sont inutiles. Ils ne savent que donner des réponses.” Cited in many places, but the source is unknown. Thus it may be fictitious.

But “AI is useless. It only knows how to give answers.” points to, in my opinion, one of the biggest steals inherent in the OpenAI post from 6 October 2026. Over the centuries, mathematicians have endeavoured to find and state open problems that can serve as guiding lights for future work. That post tackles many of them, but will AI ever furnish new ones that are as interesting as the old ones? What will work on math problems look like in the future?

Received 12 October 2026.

item.title: Keeping Mathematical Conferences Human
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: As AI makes it increasingly easy to produce polished mathematical papers, slides, and explanations, conferences may have an opportunity to become more interactive and more human. I suggest experimenting with conversational talk formats, where chairs and audiences can ask questions throughout, encouraging discussion, clarification, and a deeper shared understanding of mathematics.
item.content:encoded:
Marco Trombetti, Professor at Università degli Studi di Napoli

SERIES · AI is making papers cheap to produce but they remain costly to referee. Proofs and Prompts is publishing a series of posts from 26 October on the future of publishing, papers and credit. Questions such as how to disclose AI use, who bears the cost of checking, what authorship means and what papers of the future might look like will be addressed. This post is part of the series. Each is written independently and reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

For a long time, the standard format of a mathematical conference talk has been remarkably stable. A mathematician stands in front of a room. There are slides, or a blackboard. For twenty, thirty, or fifty minutes, the speaker explains a piece of work. At the end, if time remains, there may be a few questions. This format has always had limitations. But I wonder whether the arrival of increasingly capable AI systems gives us a new reason to reconsider it.

In a previous post, I argued that one of the important problems of AI-generated mathematics will be humanization. It is not enough that a mathematical argument exists, or even that it is correct. Someone should understand it, reorganize it, explain why it works, and connect it to the rest of mathematics. Perhaps conferences will have to adapt to the same problem.

A polished talk no longer tells us very much

Suppose I want to talk about a paper at a conference. An AI system may have helped substantially in producing the mathematics. It may have written parts of the argument, reorganized the exposition, prepared the slides, generated examples, suggested explanations, and perhaps even written the script of my talk. In principle, I could give a very polished presentation of a piece of mathematics that I understand only superficially.

Of course, something similar was possible before AI. People have always been able to present work they did not completely understand, and talks have never been examinations of their speakers. But AI changes the scale of the problem. Producing twenty beautiful slides explaining a technical argument is becoming very cheap. Producing a plausible explanation of why a theorem is interesting is becoming cheap. Producing answers to anticipated questions is becoming cheap.

Understanding the mathematics is not necessarily becoming equally cheap.

There is therefore a strange possibility: mathematical communication may become increasingly polished at exactly the same time that the connection between the person communicating the mathematics and the person (or machine) that actually produced the ideas becomes weaker. Perhaps the traditional conference talk is not particularly well designed for this situation.

What if a talk were a conversation?

I have been wondering about a different format. Imagine something closer to an interview than to a lecture. The speaker sits with a chair or moderator in front of the audience. The speaker still presents the work, perhaps with slides or a blackboard, but the presentation is not a forty-minute uninterrupted monologue. Instead, the chair interrupts.

Why did you introduce this definition?

What happens if this hypothesis is removed?

Can you explain the main idea without the technical machinery?

Where exactly does the difficult part of the proof occur?

Is this lemma really necessary?

How did you arrive at this argument?

What is the simplest example in which the phenomenon appears?

The chair would have read at least part of the paper beforehand and prepared a few questions. Members of the audience could also intervene during the discussion rather than waiting for the final three minutes. In spirit, it might look a little more like a late-night interview than a traditional mathematical lecture.

I do not mean that mathematics conferences should become entertainment shows. There need not be a desk, a band, and applause after every theorem. Although I would not completely rule out the band. The important difference would be that the presentation becomes interactive.

Understanding becomes visible

There is something that is quite difficult to fake in a sustained mathematical conversation. If you really understand an argument, you can usually move around inside it.

You can explain it from another direction. You can say which assumptions are essential. You can produce a small example. You can explain what you tried before finding the right proof. You can react when someone asks a question you did not anticipate. You can admit which part you do not understand as well as you would like.

This does not prove that you personally discovered the mathematics. Nor should it. Mathematics is collaborative, and AI will presumably become another participant in that collaboration. I do not think conferences should become detective agencies attempting to determine which sentence was written by a human and which by a machine. The interesting question is different. Has the mathematics passed through a human mind? Can the person presenting it actually discuss it? Can the result enter a mathematical community as something that people understand, rather than merely another object that has been produced?

If the answer is yes, then I care much less about whether AI was involved in obtaining it.

There would be some pressure

There is an obvious objection. This format would be more stressful. Standing in front of an audience is already stressful enough for many people. Being interrupted by a senior mathematician asking questions could make things considerably worse. I do not think this objection should be dismissed.

In particular, younger researchers should not be placed in a situation where a conference talk becomes a public oral examination. The same is true for mathematicians who are not comfortable speaking English, people who are naturally less quick in conversation, or anyone for whom this kind of interaction creates a substantial disadvantage. Understanding mathematics and performing well under pressure are not the same ability.

Any new format would have to recognize this. Perhaps junior researchers could receive some or all of the questions in advance. Perhaps the chair could meet the speaker before the session and discuss the structure of the conversation. Perhaps traditional talks could remain available for people who prefer them. Perhaps questions could be deliberately explanatory rather than adversarial. The point should not be to catch the speaker making a mistake. The point should be to create a setting in which understanding naturally becomes part of the presentation.

But perhaps a little pressure is useful

At the same time, I am not sure that all pressure is bad. If I know that presenting a paper means that someone may ask me why Lemma 4.7 is true, I have a rather strong incentive to understand Lemma 4.7 before I submit the paper. If I know that I may have to explain why a certain definition is natural, I may spend some time thinking about whether I actually know why it is natural. And if an AI system has generated an argument that I do not understand, perhaps I will be less tempted to immediately turn it into a conference submission if I know that eventually I will have to sit in front of other mathematicians and discuss it.

This seems healthy. At present, AI dramatically reduces the cost of producing mathematical text. Perhaps our institutions should increase the reward for understanding that text.

The chair would have a new role

This would also change the role of the session chair. At many conferences, chairing a session currently consists mainly of introducing the speaker, watching the clock, and saying “perhaps one last question.” In a conversational format, the chair would have a genuine intellectual role. The chair might read the paper beforehand, identify its central ideas, and prepare questions that help the audience understand what matters. A good chair could rescue a difficult presentation by asking exactly the question that half the room wants to ask but does not know how to formulate.

This work would take time, of course. But perhaps it should. We spend enormous amounts of collective time attending conferences. It seems slightly strange that so little time is usually invested in designing the actual intellectual interaction that happens there.

It might make conferences better anyway

There is another possibility. Perhaps this would be a better conference format even if AI did not exist. Many mathematical talks are extremely difficult to follow. A speaker has fifty slides and forty-five minutes, the notation accumulates, one crucial definition is missed, and twenty minutes later a significant fraction of the audience has become spectators rather than participants. A chair who can interrupt and say, “Before we continue, could you explain again what this object is supposed to represent?” might improve the talk enormously.

Questions during the presentation could reveal which ideas actually interest people. The speaker might spend less time covering every theorem in the paper and more time explaining the one idea that people will remember six months later. We might discover that the purpose of a conference was never really to reproduce the contents of papers orally. Papers are quite good at containing the contents of papers. A conference should perhaps do something else.

It should create understanding, discussion, disagreement, connections, and memories.

Conferences as part of verification

I have argued elsewhere that AI-generated mathematics may require new mechanisms of verification and humanization. Perhaps conferences could become part of that process too. Not formal verification. Not peer review. Not an examination establishing authorship. Something softer.

A result arrives in the mathematical community, and someone has to stand behind it, or perhaps better, sit beside it, and talk about it with other mathematicians. The audience sees not only a theorem and a proof, but a human being navigating the ideas around them.

Questions expose unclear points. Experts notice connections. Someone asks about a missing case. Another person suggests a simpler argument. The speaker realizes that one explanation is much better than the one in the paper.

The talk becomes another stage through which mathematical output is transformed into shared mathematical understanding.

An experiment

I certainly do not think every conference should replace all talks with interviews next year. Perhaps the format would fail completely. Maybe the speakers would hate it, or the chairs would not prepare enough. Perhaps discussions would constantly run over time. Perhaps the best researchers would turn out to be terrible interviewers and the best interviewees would not necessarily be the best mathematicians. These are good reasons to experiment rather than legislate.

A conference could try one session. Five speakers. Twenty or thirty minutes each. A chair who has received the papers beforehand. Ten minutes of presentation mixed with questions and discussion. Questions from the audience throughout. For junior participants, the questions could be discussed in advance. Then ask everyone whether they learned more.

My suspicion is that we eventually need to rethink several mathematical institutions that were built for a world in which producing mathematical text was expensive. Journals are one of them. Authorship is another. Conferences may be another.

If machines can increasingly produce papers, proofs, slides, summaries, and polished explanations, then perhaps the scarce object is no longer mathematical text. Perhaps the scarce object is understanding. And if that is true, our conferences should be designed to make understanding visible.

Received 1 October 2026.

item.title: Slow Maths
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: For a long time, I had the ideal job. As a teacher, I passed on not just mathematics, but also the taste for critical thinking, for confrontation, and the joy of discovery.
item.content:encoded:
Isabelle Gallagher, head of the French Mathematical Society

For a long time, I had the ideal job. As a teacher, I passed on not just mathematics, but also the taste for critical thinking, for confrontation, and the joy of discovery. As a researcher, I contributed my small part to the greater endeavour, alongside the wider mathematical community. I was part of this collective adventure, which I believed would never end. Slowly, insidiously, however, some flaws began to appear. We elevated colleagues to the status of heroes and heroines for their technical prowess and for the number of their publications in so called prestigious journals. We awarded an ever-increasing number of prizes, with ever-larger sums, to a small number of individuals, organisations or institutions, often focusing more on their productivity and reputation than on the substance of their work, or its inherently collective nature. We watched, amused or even flattered, as a Foundation placed a prize in dollars on a small list of mathematical problems to be solved within the millennium. And we used international competition and the lack of institutional funds as excuses to embark on a frantic race for publication, without taking the time to reflect on the fundamental purpose of our work. Over the past few months, doping has become a major issue in our profession. You can obtain it by yourself, or sometimes the institution provides unlimited access to it. At first, it was simply a matter of asking ChatGPT to check a bibliography, rephrase a paragraph, proofread a calculation or improve it. Then it became possible to ask directly to perform the calculation, or even to work out the correct calculation to perform. Now we can act as ‘super-prompters’, putting hundreds or thousands of agents to work to explore as many avenues as possible, having them correct each other’s work, letting them come up with ideas, and thus ‘crack’ one after the other doctoral subjects, problems that colleagues are working on, or those that the Clay Foundation has considered to be the most important. The ecological cost of this new way of practicing
mathematics is not addressed. What price is the mathematical community prepared to make humanity pay to answer its questions? Soon, the AI industries will have grown tired of testing and refining their models on our questions, using our very work we make available to them. In the meantime, we will have turned our profession into an ultra-doped race. In the face of this transformation, it is both urgent and essential that we return to the original purpose of our work and rethink the way we assess it. I dream of a new way of practicing mathematics, one that does not require us to resort to ‘doping’ just to stay in the race. It would be ‘slow maths’, just as there is ‘slow food’ or ‘slow tourism’. A form of maths where we have a firm control of its structure and objectives. Maths that allows us to stray down side paths which sometimes turn out to be more beautiful and more interesting than the one we originally set out to explore. Maths where we take the time to reflect, to write, to explain, and to share. This practice of ‘slow-math’ is essential because it is not the final result that matters and enables us to go further, but rather the process itself, the detours, and the collective endeavour. I am convinced that it is ‘slow-math’ that will help society progress collectively and soundly, and enable young people to continue wanting to learn, to question and to understand. This practice is now only possible if we collectively decide to put an end to the race to publish, and if we agree to value the idea that can lead to a result just as much as the techniques that finalize the proof, and just as much as proofreading, rewriting, and the sharing of ideas and methods. Only then will we be able to leave the race behind, take the time to understand things in depth, and once again practice the ideal profession.

Received 29 September 2026.
